findings.description: This bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so report data — including the seeded vendor roster object — is stored without enforced server-side encryption. Any actor obtaining object-level read access or raw storage access reads the data in cleartext.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with this bucket and no ACL is declared, so future ACL or bucket-policy changes can silently make the bucket and its objects publicly readable with no account-level guardrail to stop it.

The ledger export bucket declares no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving financial export data unencrypted at rest despite the private ACL. The ACL controls access paths but provides no protection for the stored bytes.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block guards this bucket, so the private ACL is the only barrier to exposure and can be overridden by any later policy or ACL change.

Model artifacts are stored without any server-side encryption configuration. Note the asymmetry: this bucket forwards its access logs to the KMS-encrypted audit_trail bucket, yet the artifacts themselves — the more sensitive asset — are unprotected at rest.

No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined. Operational runbooks routinely contain internal hostnames, escalation procedures, and occasionally embedded credentials, making unencrypted storage a meaningful disclosure risk.

The ACL is set to the invalid value 'lcatalogopts-delivery-write', an apparent corruption of the canned ACL 'log-delivery-write'. A malformed or misunderstood ACL on the bucket that anchors audit integrity means the intended write-only log-delivery grant is not reliably expressed, and the value should be corrected to a known canned ACL rather than left to chance.

The bucket holding audit logs for the environment has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block attached. Audit trails are high-value targets for attackers seeking to confirm or erase their activity, and this bucket lacks the account-level guardrail against accidental public exposure.

A vendor roster spreadsheet is uploaded with no kms_key_id or server_side_encryption argument into reports_archive, a bucket that itself has no default encryption. The object is therefore stored in cleartext, and vendor rosters commonly contain contact and contractual data subject to confidentiality obligations.

No bucket policy denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, so this bucket accepts plaintext HTTP requests carrying financial ledger data. The same gap applies across all buckets in this file, but is most consequential here.

Unlike the other buckets in this file, reports_archive has no versioning block. Without version history, objects such as the seeded vendor roster can be overwritten or deleted with no recoverable prior state, removing a key defence against destructive or ransomware-style tampering.
No versioning is enabled on the ledger export bucket, so financial records can be silently overwritten or deleted with no prior version retained for forensic comparison.
